qaitbay.name: Qaitbay
qaitbay.summary: Mamluk Sultan of Egypt from 1468 to 1496 who stabilized the state's economy, fought the Ottomans, and was a major patron of architecture across the region.

mujir-al-din.name: Mujir al-Din
mujir-al-din.summary: Jerusalemite qadi and historian (1456–1522) whose chronicle of Jerusalem and Hebron, written around 1495, is considered the most comprehensive source on the city's medieval history.

fernand-braudel.name: Fernand Braudel
fernand-braudel.summary: French historian (1902–1985) of the Annales School whose scholarship emphasized large-scale socioeconomic history, including works on the Mediterranean and on civilization and capitalism.

suleiman-the-magnificent.name: Suleiman the Magnificent
suleiman-the-magnificent.summary: Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566, whose long reign brought the empire's greatest economic, military and political power and reformed its legal system.

ebussuud-efendi.name: Ebussuud Efendi
ebussuud-efendi.summary: Ottoman jurist and Quran scholar who served as Shaykh al-Islam of the Ottoman Empire from 1545 to 1574, working closely with Suleiman the Magnificent to reorganize Ottoman law.

afonso-de-albuquerque.name: Afonso de Albuquerque
afonso-de-albuquerque.summary: Portuguese general and admiral who served as viceroy of Portuguese India from 1509 to 1515, conquering Goa and leading the first European raids into the Persian Gulf and Red Sea.

evliya-elebi.name: Evliya Çelebi
evliya-elebi.summary: Ottoman Turkish explorer (1611–1684) who spent over 40 years traveling through the Ottoman Empire and neighboring lands, recording his journeys in a travelogue called the Seyahatname.

tabriz.name: Tabriz
tabriz.summary: A city in northwestern Iran and capital of East Azerbaijan province, historically also known as Tauris, noted today for its handicrafts and carpet weaving.

aleppo-room.name: Aleppo Room
aleppo-room.summary: Set of carved wooden wall panels from a reception room in a house in Aleppo, Syria. A Persian artist carved them in 1603, and they were sold in 1912 and now sit in Berlin's Pergamon Museum.

as-ad-pasha-al-azm.name: As'ad Pasha al-Azm
as-ad-pasha-al-azm.summary: Ottoman governor of Damascus from 1743 until he was deposed in 1757. He was responsible for building several architectural works in the city and elsewhere in Syria.

jazzar-pasha.name: Jazzar Pasha
jazzar-pasha.summary: Ottoman governor of Sidon from 1776 until his death in 1804, based in Acre, which he strongly fortified. Born in Bosnia, he began his career serving mamluk officials in Egypt and also governed Damascus several times.

el-jazzar-mosque.name: El-Jazzar Mosque
el-jazzar-mosque.summary: Also known as the White Mosque of Acre, it stands inside the walls of the old city of Acre, Israel, overlooking the eastern Mediterranean. It is named after the Ottoman Bosnian governor Ahmad Pasha el-Jazzar.

selaml-k.name: Selamlık
selaml-k.summary: Part of an Ottoman palace or house reserved for men, where guests were received and entertained. Its name comes from the word for 'greeting'; the women's quarters were the haremlik.

harem.name: Harem
harem.summary: Domestic space reserved for the women of the house, especially in a Muslim family. It could house wives, children, female relatives and servants, and in the past enslaved concubines.

caesarea-maritima.name: Caesarea Maritima
caesarea-maritima.summary: An ancient Mediterranean port city, capital of Roman Judaea for about 650 years, founded as a Phoenician trading village and later expanded by Herod the Great.

beit-ghazaleh.name: Beit Ghazaleh
beit-ghazaleh.summary: One of the largest and best-preserved Ottoman-period palaces in Aleppo, named for the family that owned it for about two centuries. Used as a school from 1914, it was restored to host the city's Memory Museum.

saint-george-greek-orthodox-cathedral-ac.name: Saint George Greek Orthodox Cathedral
saint-george-greek-orthodox-cathedral-ac.summary: Orthodox church and monastery in Acre, Israel, dating to the 16th century and built on the ruins of a Byzantine church. It is the cathedral of the Metropolis of Ptolemais (Acre).
saint-george-greek-orthodox-cathedral-ac.source_title: Saint George Greek Orthodox Cathedral, Acre

treaty-of-zuhab.name: Treaty of Zuhab
treaty-of-zuhab.summary: Treaty signed on 17 May 1639 ending the Ottoman-Safavid War of 1623 to 1639 and fixing borders between the two empires that closely resemble today's Turkey-Iran and Iraq-Iran borders.

dagestan.name: Dagestan
dagestan.summary: A republic of Russia in the North Caucasus along the Caspian Sea, sharing borders with Azerbaijan, Georgia and several Russian republics; one of Russia's most ethnically and linguistically diverse regions.

shirvan.name: Shirvan
shirvan.summary: A historical Iranian region in the eastern Caucasus, known from the pre-Islamic Sasanian era through the early Islamic period, today part of Azerbaijan between the Caspian Sea and the Kura River.

battle-of-chaldiran.name: Battle of Chaldiran
battle-of-chaldiran.summary: A 1514 battle in which the Ottoman Empire decisively defeated the Safavids, letting the Ottomans seize Eastern Anatolia and Upper Mesopotamia and halting further Safavid expansion westward.

selim-i.name: Selim I
selim-i.summary: Ottoman sultan from 1512 to 1520, known as Selim the Grim, whose conquest of the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and the Levant made the Ottoman Empire the leading Muslim power.

nader-shah.name: Nader Shah
nader-shah.summary: Founder of Iran's Afsharid dynasty, ruling as shah from 1736 until his assassination in 1747; his campaigns built an empire stretching from India to the Caucasus.

karim-khan-zand.name: Karim Khan Zand
karim-khan-zand.summary: Founder of the Zand dynasty who ruled most of Iran from 1751 to 1779, bringing peace and prosperity after decades of war and restoring relations with Britain.

safi-of-persia.name: Shah Safi
safi-of-persia.summary: Sixth shah of Safavid Iran, ruling 1629 to 1642; a reclusive ruler who purged rivals, including a 1632 massacre of forty harem women, while losing ground to the Ottomans.

taban-yass-mehmed-pasha.name: Tabanıyassı Mehmed Pasha
taban-yass-mehmed-pasha.summary: An Ottoman statesman of Albanian descent (1589–1637) who served as Grand Vizier from 1632 under Sultan Murat IV before being executed by drowning in 1637.

fuzuli-poet.name: Fuzuli
fuzuli-poet.summary: Studied literature, mathematics, astronomy and languages as a child, and despite wishing to see Tabriz, Anatolia and India he never traveled outside Iraq; he died of the plague in 1556 and was buried in Karbala.

seyahatn-me.name: Seyahatnâme
seyahatn-me.summary: A travelogue by Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi (1611–1682) describing his journeys across the Ottoman Empire; its title became the standard Turkish word for a travel book.

isaac-luria.name: Isaac Luria
isaac-luria.summary: Jewish mystic in Safed (c. 1534–1572) considered the father of contemporary Kabbalah, even though he personally wrote only a few poems.

safed.name: Safed
safed.summary: A city in Israel's Galilee, at up to 937 m the highest in the country; fortified by Crusaders in 1168, taken by Saladin, and later a center of Jewish Kabbalah under Ottoman rule.

aq-qoyunlu.name: Aq Qoyunlu
aq-qoyunlu.summary: A Turkoman, Persian-influenced Sunni Muslim tribal confederation that ruled eastern Turkey from 1378 and later Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Iraq, peaking under Uzun Hasan.

alvand-beg.name: Alvand Mirza
alvand-beg.summary: An Aq Qoyunlu prince, grandson of Uzun Hasan, who contended for the Aq Qoyunlu throne between 1497 and 1504 or 1505.

layla-and-majnun.name: Layla and Majnun
layla-and-majnun.summary: An ancient Arab love story about the 7th-century poet Qays ibn al-Mulawwah and his lover Layla, later retold across Arabic, Persian, Turkish and Indic literature.

k-tip-elebi.name: Kâtip Çelebi
k-tip-elebi.summary: 17th-century Ottoman Turkish polymath who compiled a vast bibliographic encyclopedia of books and sciences and wrote widely in Arabic, Turkish and Persian.

hayyim-ben-joseph-vital.name: Hayyim Vital
hayyim-ben-joseph-vital.summary: A rabbi in Safed (1542–1620) and the foremost disciple of Isaac Luria, who recorded much of his master's teachings, which later had a powerful impact across the Jewish world.

melay-ciz-r.name: Melayê Cizîrî
melay-ciz-r.summary: Kurdish poet, theologian, and Sufi mystic, born around 1570 in Cizre and died around 1640 in Diyarbakır.

gorani-language.name: Gurani
gorani-language.summary: A Northwestern Iranian language or group of dialects spoken in small pockets of Iraq and Iran, whose main dialect, Hawrami, was once a literary language for Kurds.

avroman.name: Hawraman
avroman.summary: A mountainous region straddling western Iran and northeastern Iraq, home to the Hawrami Kurdish people, known for terraced farming and seasonal migration between highlands and lowlands.

yarsanism.name: Yarsanism
yarsanism.summary: A syncretic monotheistic religion founded by Sultan Sahak in western Iran in the late 14th century, whose god manifests in one primary form and six secondary ones, together called the Holy Seven.

revolt-of-zulfiqar-khan.name: Ibrahim Khan
revolt-of-zulfiqar-khan.summary: The Safavid governor of Iranian Kurdistan, killed in Baghdad in 1528 by his own nephew, Zulfiqar Khan, during a pro-Ottoman revolt.

hillah.name: Hillah
hillah.summary: A city in central Iraq on the Euphrates near ancient Babylon, once a major center of Islamic scholarship and later a key administrative city under Ottoman and Mandatory Iraq.

imam-ali-shrine.name: Imam Ali Shrine
imam-ali-shrine.summary: The mausoleum of Ali, cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad, in Najaf, Iraq—considered the holiest site in Shia Islam after Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem.

smyrna.name: Smyrna
smyrna.summary: An ancient Greek city on the Aegean coast of Anatolia, renamed İzmir in 1930, with remains from the Archaic and Roman periods still found within the modern city.

zhovkva.name: Zolkiev
zhovkva.summary: The historical Polish name for Zhovkva, a city now in Lviv Oblast, western Ukraine, with a population of about 13,852.

isaac-satanow.name: Isaac Satanow
isaac-satanow.summary: Polish-Jewish scholar and poet (1732–1804), a maskil of the Jewish Enlightenment.

maronites.name: Maronites
maronites.summary: Syriac Christian ethnoreligious group native to the Levant, especially Lebanon's Mount Lebanon, named after the monk Saint Maron and belonging to the Maronite Church.

tripoli-eyalet.name: Tripoli Eyalet
tripoli-eyalet.summary: An Ottoman province (eyalet) centered on Tripoli, Lebanon, covering the coastal towns and mountain areas of what is now northern Lebanon and coastal Syria.

fakhr-al-din-ii.name: Fakhr al-Din II
fakhr-al-din-ii.summary: Druze emir of Mount Lebanon and Ottoman governor from the 1590s to 1633 who united the region's Druze and Maronite communities and is regarded as Lebanon's founder.

battle-of-marj-dabiq.name: Battle of Marj Dabiq
battle-of-marj-dabiq.summary: A 24 August 1516 battle near Aleppo in which the Ottomans crushed the Mamluk Sultanate, gaining control of Syria and opening the way to conquer Egypt.

mount-lebanon.name: Mount Lebanon
mount-lebanon.summary: A mountain range in Lebanon known for its snow-capped peaks and cedar forests, the source of the country's name.

ottoman-safavid-war-1623-1639.name: Ottoman–Safavid War (1623–1639)
ottoman-safavid-war-1623-1639.summary: Conflict from 1623 to 1639 between the Ottoman and Safavid empires over Mesopotamia; the Safavids retook Baghdad after 90 years but the Ottomans recaptured it, ending the war with the Treaty of Zuhab.

safavid-dynasty.name: Safavid dynasty
safavid-dynasty.summary: Ruling dynasty of Safavid Iran from 1501 to 1736, of Kurdish origin based in Ardabil; Shah Ismail I made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion, a turning point in Islamic history.

ferdinando-i-de-medici.name: Ferdinando I de' Medici
ferdinando-i-de-medici.summary: Grand Duke of Tuscany from 1587 to 1609 who fostered Tuscan culture, supported Henry IV of France, and pursued canal and irrigation projects.

battle-of-ridaniya.name: Battle of Ridaniya
battle-of-ridaniya.summary: A 22 January 1517 battle in Egypt in which Ottoman forces under Selim I defeated the Mamluks under Tuman bay II, ending the Mamluk Sultanate and bringing Egypt under Ottoman rule.

damascus-eyalet.name: Damascus Eyalet
damascus-eyalet.summary: An Ottoman province covering Syria, created after the Ottomans took the region from the Mamluks in 1516–1517, later reorganized into the Syria Vilayet by 1867.

sanjak.name: Sanjak
sanjak.summary: An administrative division of the Ottoman Empire, rooted in the Turkic and Mongol steppe tradition of organizing by banners, headed by a bey.

ma-n-dynasty.name: Ma'n dynasty
ma-n-dynasty.summary: Family of Druze chiefs of Arab descent based in the Chouf area of Mount Lebanon, politically prominent from the 15th to 17th centuries.

shihab-dynasty.name: Shihab dynasty
shihab-dynasty.summary: An Arab family that served as paramount tax farmers and emirs of Mount Lebanon under Ottoman rule, from the early 18th to mid-19th century.

bashir-shihab-ii.name: Bashir Shihab II
bashir-shihab-ii.summary: Emir who ruled the Emirate of Mount Lebanon from 1788 to 1840, the only Maronite ruler among the Shihab dynasty, which had converted from Sunni Islam.

ottoman-iraq.name: Ottoman Iraq
ottoman-iraq.summary: The Ottoman-controlled region of Iraq from Süleyman I's 1534 conquest until British occupation in 1917, administered through provinces such as Baghdad, Basra, Mosul and Shahrizor.

peace-of-amasya.name: Peace of Amasya
peace-of-amasya.summary: An 1555 treaty between Safavid Iran and the Ottoman Empire that ended their 1532 to 1555 war, dividing the Caucasus between the two powers.

ahmad-ma-n.name: Ahmad Ma'n
ahmad-ma-n.summary: Paramount emir of the Druze in Mount Lebanon from 1667 until his death in 1697, and the last ruler of the Ma'n dynasty, after which power passed to the Shihab family.

chouf-district.name: Chouf
chouf-district.summary: A historic mountainous district of Lebanon, in the governorate of Mount Lebanon, long a stronghold of Druze leadership.

keserwan-district.name: Keserwan
keserwan-district.summary: A district in Lebanon northeast of Beirut whose capital, Jounieh, is overwhelmingly Christian and mostly Maronite; it is home to the Jabal Moussa Biosphere Reserve.

beylik-of-dulkadir.name: Beylik of Dulkadir
beylik-of-dulkadir.summary: Turkish Anatolian principality established by Oghuz Turk clans after the decline of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm, later serving as a buffer state between the Ottomans and Mamluks.

eyalet.name: Eyalet
eyalet.summary: A major administrative province of the Ottoman Empire from 1453 until the early 19th century, governed by a beylerbey with broad military, financial and judicial powers.

sidon-eyalet.name: Eyalet of Safed
sidon-eyalet.summary: An Ottoman provincial administrative unit (eyalet) in the Levant, known as the Eyalet of Safed when its capital was there, later renamed Sidon; it extended from Egypt's border into modern Israel and Lebanon.

emirate-of-mount-lebanon.name: Mount Lebanon Emirate
emirate-of-mount-lebanon.summary: A part of Mount Lebanon with partial autonomy under Ottoman rule from the mid-16th to early 19th century, ruled first from Baakleen, then Deir el Qamar, then the Beiteddine palace.

iltizam.name: Iltizam
iltizam.summary: An Ottoman tax-farming system begun in the 15th century under Mehmed the Conqueror, in which holders taxed peasants for profit; it was abolished in 1856.

yusuf-sayfa.name: Yusuf Sayfa
yusuf-sayfa.summary: Chieftain and tax farmer (c. 1510–1625) who repeatedly served as Ottoman governor of Tripoli Eyalet from 1579, and rival of Fakhr al-Din II.

kabbalah.name: Kabbalah
kabbalah.summary: Esoteric school of Jewish mysticism forming the basis of mystical interpretation of Jewish scripture, emerging in 12th-13th century Occitania.

lurianic-kabbalah.name: Lurianic Kabbalah
lurianic-kabbalah.summary: A school of Jewish mysticism developed by rabbi Isaac Luria (1534-1572), giving a new account of Creation through concepts like the World of Tohu-Chaos and World of Tikun-Rectification.

sabbatai-zevi.name: Sabbatai Zevi
sabbatai-zevi.summary: A Jewish mystic and rabbi (1626–1676) who claimed to be the Messiah and gained a huge following, before being forced to convert to Islam in 1666 on the order of the Ottoman grand vizier, acting for Sultan Mehmed IV.

nathan-of-gaza.name: Nathan of Gaza
nathan-of-gaza.summary: A 17th-century theologian (1643–1680) who became famous as the prophet who proclaimed Sabbatai Zevi the Jewish Messiah.

sabbateans.name: Sabbateans
sabbateans.summary: Followers of Sabbatai Zevi who kept believing he was the Messiah even after his forced conversion to Islam, a movement that spread through Europe into the 18th century.

ari-ashkenazi-synagogue.name: Ari Ashkenazi Synagogue
ari-ashkenazi-synagogue.summary: A synagogue in Safed, Israel, built in the late 16th century in memory of the kabbalist Rabbi Isaac Luria, possibly the oldest synagogue in Israel still in use.

the-world-of-chaos-and-the-world-of-rect.name: The World of Chaos and The World of Rectification
the-world-of-chaos-and-the-world-of-rect.summary: Two stages of the spiritual worlds in Lurianic Kabbalah, developed by Isaac Luria (1534–1572) from his reading of the Zohar, representing chaotic and corrected states of Creation, free will and redemption.
the-world-of-chaos-and-the-world-of-rect.source_title: The World of Chaos and The World of Rectification

zohar.name: Zohar
zohar.summary: A foundational work of Kabbalistic Jewish mysticism, first publicized around 1280-1286 by Moses de León, though traditionally attributed to a 2nd-century sage.

jacob-frank.name: Jacob Frank
jacob-frank.summary: Polish-Jewish religious leader (1726–1791) who claimed to be a reincarnation of Sabbatai Zevi and founded the syncretic movement known as Frankism.

pope-gregory-xiii.name: Pope Gregory XIII
pope-gregory-xiii.summary: Born Ugo Boncompagni, head of the Catholic Church from 1572 to 1585; best known for commissioning the Gregorian calendar still used today.

pontifical-maronite-college.name: Pontifical Maronite College
pontifical-maronite-college.summary: One of the Roman Colleges of the Catholic Church, founded in 1584 to educate Maronite priests; it now also serves priests from other Eastern denominations.

maronite-church.name: Maronite Church
maronite-church.summary: Eastern Catholic church in full communion with the pope, headquartered near Beirut, Lebanon, with roots going back to Saint Maron and the Monastery of Saint Maroun in the 4th to 7th centuries.

d-nmeh.name: Dönmeh
d-nmeh.summary: A group of Ottoman crypto-Jews who outwardly converted to Islam in the 17th century after their leader Shabbetai Tzevi did so, secretly keeping Jewish and Kabbalistic beliefs; many later became prominent Turkish nationalists.

baruchiah-russo.name: Baruchiah Russo
baruchiah-russo.summary: Baruchiah Russo (1677–1720): Sabbatean leader of the Karakas community and successor to Sabbatai Zevi.

jacob-ben-aaron-sasportas.name: Jacob ben Aaron Sasportas
jacob-ben-aaron-sasportas.summary: Algerian-born rabbi, kabbalist, diplomat, and author (1610–1698) who served Jewish communities in North Africa and Europe, including London and Amsterdam.

jacob-hagiz.name: Jacob Hagiz
jacob-hagiz.summary: Jewish Talmudist (1620–1674) born to a Sephardic family in Fez, Morocco.
